title: Incident Report: Outage of the Production Planning System

content.text: Incident Report: Outage of the Production Planning System

Report number INC-2026-0417, prepared by [PERSON_2], Incident Manager, with contributions from [PERSON_1], IT Operations Lead. Status: final, approved by the IT steering committee on [DATE_1]. Distribution: management board, plant managers, IT department and works council.
Summary

On [DATE_2], the production planning system of [ORG_1] was unavailable for a total of 6 hours and 40 minutes, from 05:52 to 12:32. During the outage, the production lines at the main plant in [LOCATION_1] and at the plant in [LOCATION_2] could not receive updated production orders, work instructions or material staging requests. Both plants continued to work on the basis of the orders already released for the early shift, but from around 08:30 several lines had to be stopped or switched to manual planning.

The direct cause of the outage was a full transaction log on the database server of the production planning system after a failed nightly backup job. The backup job had failed because the credentials of its service account had expired, and the monitoring alert for the failed job was sent to a mailbox that nobody had been watching since a reorganisation of the IT operations team. This report describes the course of events, the impact on production, the root cause analysis and the measures agreed to prevent a similar outage in the future.
No data was lost, and there are no indications of a security incident. Customer deliveries were delayed by one to two days for 23 orders; no delivery penalties were incurred.

Impact on Customers and Finances

The lost output was recovered over the following four working days through additional Saturday shifts at both plants. Despite this, 23 customer orders were delivered one to two days late. The sales team informed the affected customers proactively on the day of the outage. The total cost of the outage, including overtime supplements, lost productivity and additional freight, is estimated at
. This figure does not include the working time of the IT staff involved in the response.
Impact on Data

The data in the production planning system is complete. Operations that were carried out during the outage were recorded on paper and entered manually by the shift supervisors between 12:32 and 16:00. A reconciliation of production confirmations with the ERP system on the following day showed no differences.
Root Cause Analysis

The root cause analysis was carried out in a post-incident review on [DATE_3] with the IT operations team, the database administrators, the service desk and representatives of both plants. The review followed a blameless format: the aim was to understand how the systems and processes allowed the outage to happen, not to find individuals at fault.
Immediate Cause

The production planning database runs in full recovery mode. In this mode, the transaction log is only truncated after a successful log backup. Because the backup job had failed for three consecutive nights, the transaction log kept growing until it reached the maximum file size of 200 GB at 05:52. From that moment, the database could no longer process write transactions, and all functions that confirm operations or create staging requests stopped working.
Contributing Factors
The review identified several contributing factors that together turned a routine backup problem into a major outage:

The service account used by the backup job had a password expiry of 365 days, which had not been documented. Service accounts are supposed to be exempt from expiry, but this account was created before the current policy came into force.
Alerts for failed backup jobs were still sent to the mailbox of the former database team, which was dissolved in a reorganisation six months ago. Nobody had been reading this mailbox since then.
There was no monitoring of the transaction log size, although the vendor recommends a warning at 70 percent and a critical alert at 85 percent.

The service desk initially classified the outage as priority 3 because the first report came from a single line and looked like a terminal problem. The escalation to priority 1 took 1 hour and 30 minutes.
The runbook for the production planning system did not contain instructions for a full transaction log, so the on-call administrator had to analyse the problem from scratch.
Why the Recovery Took So Long

Once the cause was known, the team decided to perform a full backup before truncating the log. This decision was correct, as it ensured that the database could be restored if the truncation failed, but the backup took more than two hours because it was written to the slower archive storage. A backup to the faster primary backup storage would have taken around 40 minutes but was not possible because this storage was also nearly full.
Response and Recovery

The incident team worked effectively once it had been set up. Communication with the plants via the plant managers and the shift supervisors was described as clear and timely in the feedback from both sites. The decision to switch to manual planning was taken jointly by the incident manager and the plant managers at 08:30 and prevented a complete stop of production. The paper-based fallback procedure from the business continuity plan was used for the first time in a real incident and worked largely as intended, although the printed order lists in [LOCATION_2] were not up to date and had to be supplemented by phone.

The restart of the database and the reprocessing of the ERP interface queue went smoothly. The shift supervisors entered all paper records on the same day, so that the system was fully up to date for the late shift.
Corrective and Preventive Actions
The following actions were agreed in the post-incident review. Progress is tracked in the IT service portal under the problem record PRB-2026-0089.
Convert all service accounts to managed accounts without password expiry and document them in the configuration management database. Owner: [PERSON_1]. Due: [DATE_4].
Redirect all alerts from the former database team mailbox to the IT operations ticket queue and review all other alert recipients for outdated addresses. Owner: [PERSON_3]. Due: [DATE_5].

Introduce monitoring of the transaction log size and the free disk space for all production databases, with warning and critical thresholds as recommended by the vendor. Owner: [PERSON_3]. Due: [DATE_5].
Extend the primary backup storage by 4 TB so that full backups can always be written to fast storage. Owner: [PERSON_1]. Due: [DATE_6].
Add a section on database storage problems to the runbook of the production planning system and train all on-call administrators. Owner: [PERSON_4]. Due: [DATE_6].

Update the service desk triage guide: any report of terminals failing on a production line is to be classified as priority 2 at least and escalated to priority 1 if a second line or site reports the same problem. Owner: [PERSON_2]. Due: [DATE_4].
Review and update the printed fallback order lists at both plants weekly as part of the business continuity plan. Owner: plant managers. Due: [DATE_5].
Lessons Learned

This outage did not have a single cause; it was the result of several small gaps that had accumulated over time. A reorganisation changed responsibilities, but the technical configuration, such as alert recipients, was not adapted. We will therefore add a checklist for technical handovers to our change process for future reorganisations.

The incident also showed that our business continuity plan works in principle, and that the cooperation between IT and the plants during a crisis is good. At the same time, it reminded us that the production planning system is now as critical for our plants as the machines themselves. We will review whether the system should be operated in a high-availability configuration and present a proposal with costs to the IT steering committee by the end of the next quarter.
